Subject: PayFlux live assistant — latency & streaming follow-up

Hi Samira / Luca — thanks again for the call today. Short recap and proposed next steps so we keep momentum: 

Call highlights
- Primary goal: integrate an on-demand support assistant during payments flow (authorization & dispute triage).
- Target TTFT (time-to-first-token): goal <= 120 ms for 95th percentile on interactive flows; acceptable up to 200 ms for long-form outputs (background ops).
- Streaming: you prefer server-sent events (SSE) for browser clients; asked about WebSocket fallback for mobile/webviews.
- Chunk cadence: you called out a desire for partial results every ~200-400 ms for user-perceived responsiveness.
- Concurrency/throughput: preliminary expectation ~150 concurrent users during peak, ~250 rps spike capacity; average payload ~800-1,500 tokens per response.

Proposed next steps
1) Redwood runs a baseline probe against a synthetic workload (we'll use the harness linked below) to establish TTFT and chunk cadence behavior with your expected token sizes.
2) PayFlux to share recent traffic profile (RPS per minute, typical prompt lengths, auth flow timing) and confirm which endpoints will call the assistant.
3) We propose an initial pilot window (2 business days) where we run 1) with your staging environment and then iterate on chunk pacing and concurrency settings.

Deliverables from Redwood for pilot- a test harness + instructions (link below)- an initial perf spec worksheet (attached)- suggested default cadence: 250 ms chunk cadence, SSE preferred with WS fallback, optimistic concurrency limit 50 simultaneous decoding sessions per replica

Samira — can you confirm the expected peak RPS and whether the assistant will be proxied through your edge infra or call Redwood directly? Also please share the traffic profile CSV and any strict TTFT SLAs from product.

Ben
Ben Carter
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Thanks Ben — quick clarifications: 
- Peak RPS: our SREs are seeing ~220 rps sustained for the payments ui during promotions; peak spikes up to ~400 rps for short windows (1–2 minutes).
- Concurrent users: peak concurrent sessions hitting the assistant are closer to 200 (browser tabs + mobile) but not all are active simultaneously; conservatively we should design for 120 active decodes.
- Traffic path: we'll proxy through our edge (EdgeInfra) for auth and rate limits; low-latency requests (payments flow) can be routed to Redwood via our private peering if you support it.
- Token sizes: typical responses average 1,100 tokens; in some customer support cases it can be 2,500 tokens.

Two asks from our side:
1) If the 95th percentile TTFT target is <= 120 ms, what configuration (replica size, concurrency per replica, and batching window) would you recommend for ~250 rps baseline?
2) For SSE chunk cadence, can you provide guidance on how to avoid reflow/UX jitter for our frontend when partial chunks arrive at 200–300 ms intervals?

Samira
Product Lead — Conversational Experiences, PayFlux

Subject: Re: PayFlux live assistant — latency & streaming follow-up

Samira / Luca — thanks for the detail, that's very helpful. TL;DR: we can likely meet your 95p TTFT <=120 ms target for short responses with the right replica and concurrency mix; long-form (2,500 tokens) will be higher due to decode time.

Answers to your asks:
1) Recommended starting configuration for ~250 rps baseline:
- Replica: medium (16GB GPU mem / optimized kernel profile)
- Concurrency per replica: start at 50 active decodes; autoscale target up to 120 when queue latency rises
- Batching: continuous batching with 8–12 ms pack window for small prompts; disable large batching for long-form to avoid TTFT regression
- Cache: enable prefix/KV caching for repeated prompts (we can instrument hit-rate quickly)

2) SSE chunk cadence UX guidance:
- Use a 250 ms cadence as the default; 150 ms is aggressive and increases CPU scheduling overhead and network chattiness.
- Send a small "keepalive/frame" first packet (fast, ~20–40 tokens) so the UI can render a token skeleton and avoid layout jumps when the larger chunk arrives.
- Coalesce very small token bursts into a single chunk if arrival time delta < 40 ms to reduce reflow.
- Provide a client-side aggregator that buffers for up to 120 ms before committing to DOM updates; this smooths jitter without losing responsiveness.

Next steps
- We'll run the three replica/concurrency probes (Karthik owning). Please confirm the staging endpoint and whether private peering will be enabled for the pilot.
- Suggested pilot dates: Jul 14–15 (two business days). We will share results and suggested rollout settings within 48 hours of probe completion.
